overview: In 1971, a United Nations resolution known as Resolution 2758 gave China's seat at the UN to the government in Beijing. This bill adds to an existing 2019 Taiwan law a statement that the resolution did not decide Taiwan's status or its representation at the UN, and that the U.S. opposes changing Taiwan's status without the consent of its people. It directs U.S. representatives in international organizations to resist Chinese efforts to change those organizations' language or policies about Taiwan, and to encourage allies to oppose efforts to undermine Taiwan's diplomatic ties. It also adds information on China's attempts to block Taiwan's participation in international bodies to an existing State Department report. As of October 30, 2025, a Senate committee had approved it and it was placed on the Senate's calendar, meaning it is eligible for a vote by the full Senate.
for: Supporters say China uses a misreading of the 1971 resolution to push Taiwan out of international bodies, and this bill sets the record straight and directs U.S. diplomats to push back.
against: Critics say formally restating the resolution's meaning in law could heighten tensions with China, while doing little on its own to win Taiwan new roles in international organizations.
